claims.text: Formation of a single-phase noble metal–based HEA nanoparticle under rapid thermal cycling is governed by competition between short-time interdiffusion and thermodynamic driving forces for segregation.
Short high-temperature pulses can promote localized elemental ordering through favorable enthalpic interactions and differences in surface energy.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure or an uninterrupted thermal cycle permits excessive diffusion that causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
Conventional rapid heating and cooling of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles typically produces elemental segregation and incomplete structural homogenization.
Conventional rapid heating and cooling typically produces uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
Sequential short high-temperature dwell periods can be used to control local elemental ensembles in an HEA.
Rapid quenching between successive high-temperature pulses preserves the local structures formed during each pulse.
The proposed intervention applies to systems containing more than five elements.
Differences in elemental mixing enthalpies and surface energies govern the formation of nanoscale elemental clusters during pulsed annealing.
Nanoscale elemental clusters act as organizing centers that mediate selection of the overall single-phase crystal structure.
Limited diffusion during each pulse permits favorable pairwise or small-cluster interactions among elements with lower mixing enthalpies.
Brief pulses balance kinetic limitations against thermodynamic segregation sufficiently to select a uniform single-phase solid solution.
Overdevelopment of local elemental clusters drives macroscopic phase separation.
Pulsed annealing will improve atomic-level homogeneity relative to an uninterrupted rapid-heating/cooling baseline.
Pulsed annealing will reduce elemental segregation and secondary phases relative to the baseline.
Pulsed annealing will produce a more clearly defined single-phase crystal structure.
The proposed mechanism is applicable when differences in atomic size, surface energy, and mixing enthalpy are significant.
Pulses that are too short permit no useful diffusion, whereas pulses that are too long permit complete phase separation.
